worst_places.after: Where it falls short: a generic `IRepository<T>` interface works well for simple CRUD (create, read, update, delete). It stops working once one use case needs a complex query - a join, pagination, or an aggregation. You then have two bad options. Either you bloat the generic interface with dozens of specialized methods, or people bypass the repository and query the ORM (object-relational mapper) directly. Most real codebases take a third route: keep the generic base thin and add specialized query methods to each concrete repository.

patterns: THE ONE THAT EXPLAINS THE 29.4 vs 13.5 GAP - the articles use a template with slots for non-prose, the bank does not. Every article follows: scope note -> problem -> bad code -> ASCII diagram -> concept + code -> file tree -> test -> bullet list of 'when to use' -> bulleted interview traps. Enumerations land in bullets, structures land in diagrams, and a code fence arrives every third paragraph, so the prose never has to carry more than one idea at a time. The bank's template is: thesis heading -> 2 dense theory paragraphs -> one code block -> 1-2 more dense paragraphs -> one 'Common pitfall' paragraph. It has no slot for a bullet list and no slot for a diagram (only q-13 has one, in 25 answers). So every list the author wants to give becomes a semicolon chain inside one sentence, and every trade-off becomes a 'but ... which ... so ...' chain. The proof that this is format and not language skill: the RU articles have 0.0-2.7% over-long sentences (three of the seven have literally zero), while the same author's RU bank has 45.5%. Same subject, same author, same month - the only variable is that one output has bullets and diagrams available and the other does not.

The second half of the same gap: the bank has to be self-contained per answer, so each answer re-compresses a whole article into ~400 words. Article 05 spends 741 RU words on Repository with an interface, a Prisma implementation, a diagram, a test, and a NestJS mapping; bank q-3 delivers the same content in two 70-word paragraphs plus one code block. Compression, not carelessness, is what produces the 63.8% over-long-sentence rate in the EN bank. The fix is not to cut content - it is to let the bank answers use bullets, sub-headings and a second diagram the way the articles do.

Every article opens with a 'Scope note / Область применения' blockquote that says what the article does NOT cover, before it has said what the thing is. Seven of eight articles do this identically. Article 02 goes further and opens with 1970s Smalltalk history before defining the third component; article 04 opens with trivia about why the hexagon has six sides. The pyramid is inverted at the top of almost every file.

Article 08 breaks the series' own format: 4,443 EN / 3,540 RU words, 25 answers, and zero code blocks and zero diagrams - the only article of the eight with none. Its paragraphs run to 17 lines and enumerate four problems and four fixes inside prose. It reads like the question bank, not like articles 01-07, and it scores like the question bank too.

The quiz bank is not measuring knowledge. correctIndex is 0 in 16/20 items and 1 in the other 4 - positions 2 and 3 are never correct. The correct option is the longest of the four in 17/20 EN items and 16/20 RU items. Either heuristic alone scores 80-85% without reading a single question. On top of that, several explanations refer to 'Option B', 'Option C', 'Option D' (quiz-11, 12, 13, 14, 15) while the options themselves are rendered as an unlettered list, so the reader has to count positions to decode the explanation.

Content coverage mismatch between the quiz and the articles: 9 of the 20 quiz items (2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 13, 15, 16, 18) test CQRS and Event Sourcing, and neither term appears anywhere in the eight articles. A reader who works through the topic in order meets CQRS for the first time in a quiz, with the acronym unexpanded in two of those items. The question bank does cover CQRS (q-12) and the outbox pattern, so the gap is specifically article-side.
notes: Sharpest split on the site so far: articles 01-07 in both locales are close to shippable (RU 01/02/05/06/07 have literally 0-2 over-long sentences each), while article 08, the whole question bank and the whole quiz bank need a full language pass. Rubric C is the bank's strongest criterion, not its weakest: the senior/advanced answers open with thesis headings ('A Saga gives up atomicity on purpose - that's the whole point, not a compromise') that answer before explaining, and no answer lead exceeds 30 words. The middle-tier answers (q-1..q-8) are inconsistent with this and use plain label headings ('### Repository vs Service Layer'). Rubric D for this abstract topic holds up well in articles 01-07: every pattern gets a diagram or a code sketch before the next pattern arrives, and the ACL, Unit of Work, Strangler Fig and Modular Monolith sections are all example-first. E was scored 2 for article 08 in both locales because a 4k-word article about code contains no code block at all.
